summaries.example: Imagine a caring parent who wants a child to grow into a kind and brave person. The parent may allow the child to face a difficult challenge instead of fixing every problem immediately. Some philosophers compare this with the idea that God may allow hardship for reasons humans do not fully understand. Other philosophers ask whether any reason could make terrible suffering acceptable.
summaries.summary: Divine providence is the belief that God guides the world. The entry asks how this belief can fit with the existence of evil. It discusses two kinds of evil: moral evil, which comes from wrong choices, and natural evil, which comes from nature and causes such as illness or accidents. One response says that free will is a great good, even though it allows people to do wrong. Other responses discuss God’s knowledge of the future, the possibility that God knows what free creatures would do in different situations, and the view that God controls creation while creatures can still act freely. The entry also considers whether suffering can help people grow in virtue and whether evil can be overcome rather than merely balanced by good. Some thinkers reply that human beings may be unable to see God’s reasons. The discussion does not present one agreed answer; it shows why the problem is difficult.
key_ideas: Traditional belief about God describes God as knowing everything, having unlimited power, and being perfectly good.
The world contains beauty and goodness, but also wrongdoing, suffering, destruction, and death.
Some philosophers argue that free choices explain much moral evil: meaningful freedom includes the possibility of choosing badly.
Other views say God may know every future choice, may discover some future choices as they happen, or may control creation in a deeper way.
Some theodicies say that facing hardship can help people develop courage, compassion, patience, and other virtues.
The entry ends by saying that no explanation is complete and that mystery may remain.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects big religious ideas with everyday questions about fairness, pain, choice, and responsibility. It can help us understand why people disagree about God without treating disagreement as foolish. It also asks how we should act when suffering happens: with courage, compassion, forgiveness, and efforts to reduce harm. Studying the problem does not require accepting one answer.

important_terms.definition: The idea that God guides and governs everything that happens in the world.
The problem of explaining how suffering and wrongdoing can exist if God is all-knowing, all-powerful, and perfectly good.
The ability to choose and act for oneself rather than being forced by earlier causes.
Wrongdoing caused by the choices of thinking beings, such as lying or hurting someone on purpose.
Harm that comes from nature or events not directly caused by someone’s wrongdoing, such as disease or an earthquake.
The idea that a bad thing can be overcome within a much greater good, rather than simply being traded for a good result.

questions_to_think_about: Could people be truly free if they were never able to choose wrongly?
Is suffering always useful, or might some suffering seem to have no clear purpose?
Can not knowing a reason for something prove that there is no reason?
Would a world with only pleasure be the best kind of world?
How should people respond when others are suffering?

summaries.example: Suppose a person freely decides whether to attend a concert, and imagine that this decision later affects many other people. A view called open theism says that, before the choice occurs, even God may not know its definite outcome, though God can estimate possibilities and guide circumstances. A Molinist view says God knows, before creating anything, what that person would freely choose in every possible situation. The traditional view discussed in the entry says God is the first cause of the person and the decision, yet the decision can still be genuinely voluntary. Each proposal tries to reconcile freedom with divine omniscience and sovereignty, but each faces objections.
summaries.summary: The entry examines divine providence through the problem of evil. Traditional theism attributes omniscience, omnipotence, and perfect goodness to God, yet the world contains moral evil, natural suffering, destruction, and death. The logical problem claims these facts are inconsistent; responses argue that the contradiction follows only if every evil must lack a divine justification. The evidential problem is more cautious: the extent and apparent pointlessness of suffering may make traditional theism unlikely, although humans may not be able to judge whether every evil has a reason or whether goods and evils can be measured on one scale. The free will defense holds that moral evil results from libertarian choices and that meaningful freedom may be worth the risk, but this appears to limit God’s sovereignty or foreknowledge. Open theism preserves creaturely freedom by treating some future choices as unsettled, while middle knowledge attempts to preserve stronger providence through truths about what creatures would do in possible circumstances. The entry questions whether such truths can be known or justified. A traditional alternative places all creaturely actions under God’s creative authority and argues, through an author-and-story analogy, that divine causation need not operate like coercion within the created world. It then considers whether evil and suffering can be defeated through moral transformation, justice, compassion, and the development of virtue. Finally, skeptical theism and related appeals to mystery caution against inferring that no divine reason exists merely because humans cannot find one. key_ideas: The logical problem of evil claims that divine perfection and evil cannot coexist; a reply says this conclusion needs the extra assumption that no good reason could justify allowing evil.

The evidential problem argues from the scale, intensity, and apparently pointless distribution of suffering. Its critics question whether humans should expect to recognize all possible divine reasons.
The free will defense separates moral evil from natural evil and argues that valuable libertarian freedom carries the risk of wrongful choice.
Free will creates pressure on divine omniscience and sovereignty: if choices are not determined, can God know them infallibly and control the whole history of creation?

Open theism accepts significant uncertainty for God, while Molinism seeks providential control through counterfactuals about what creatures would freely do. The entry raises problems about how such counterfactuals could be justified.

The traditional solution gives God complete creative authority and tries to preserve creaturely freedom through a special relation between God’s creative activity and human agency, rather than ordinary event-causation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it tests whether a set of influential claims can fit together: that God governs creation, that people are responsible agents, and that the world contains severe suffering. It also clarifies different argumentative tasks. A defense may show that belief is logically consistent without showing that it is probable or emotionally satisfying. Theories of providence further affect how we understand blame, prayer, responsibility, hope, and responses to suffering. Comparing the proposals helps readers distinguish a proof, an explanation, a defense, and an acknowledgment of mystery.

important_terms.definition: The traditional claim that God knows every truth, including truths about the past, present, and future.
The traditional claim that God can do anything that is logically possible.
The claim that God is perfectly good and always intends the best possible outcome.
An argument that the amount and distribution of evil provide evidence against the existence of a perfectly good, all-powerful, all-knowing God.
Freedom understood as action not determined by prior conditions that guarantee what a person will choose; it is linked to responsibility.
The view that God does not know future free choices as settled facts before they occur, though God can know probabilities and guide circumstances.
The proposed divine knowledge of what any possible free creature would do in every possible circumstance, before God chooses what to create.
A view in which God’s creative activity is the first cause of creatures and their actions, while defenders argue that this need not make creatures passive or unfree.

questions_to_think_about: Does the existence of apparently pointless suffering support an evidential argument against traditional theism, or does human epistemic limitation weaken that argument?
Can libertarian freedom be compatible with God’s complete creative control?
What justification would God have for knowing what a merely possible creature would freely do?
Is a world containing challenge and suffering morally better than a world designed only to maximize pleasure?
Does saying that evil may be a mystery answer the problem, or only explain why a full answer may be unavailable?

summaries.example: Imagine a coach who lets players make their own choices during a game. The coach may know their habits and plan carefully, but a player can still choose a surprising move. One philosopher might say the coach cannot know that move for certain until it happens. Another might say the coach already knows what the player would choose in every possible situation. A third might say the coach’s role is so deep that the player’s free action is part of the coach’s overall plan without being forced in the ordinary way. These examples show why philosophers debate freedom, knowledge, and control.
summaries.summary: Divine providence concerns the idea that God governs the world. The entry focuses on the problem of evil: how can a perfectly knowing, powerful, and good God preside over a world containing wrongdoing, suffering, destruction, and death? It first separates two arguments. The logical argument says these claims cannot all be true together. The evidential argument says the amount and apparent pointlessness of evil make traditional theism unlikely. A response to both arguments is that humans may not be able to identify every good reason God could have for permitting evil. The free will defense explains moral evil through libertarian freedom, the idea that choices are not fixed by earlier conditions. It argues that freedom and freely given love may be valuable enough to justify the risk of wrongdoing, but critics ask whether this sacrifices divine control or knowledge. Open theism accepts an unsettled future, while middle knowledge claims that God knows what every possible free creature would do in every possible situation. The entry questions how this special knowledge could be justified. The traditional approach gives God complete creative authority and argues that God can be the source of creatures and their actions without forcing them as an external cause. The entry also examines theodicies based on soul-making, in which hardship can develop courage and compassion, and on the defeat of evil, in which evil is addressed within a greater good rather than merely exchanged for one. It ends by considering mystery: not seeing a divine reason may not prove that no reason exists. Still, this is not a complete explanation of every case, so the philosophical problem remains open.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes a logical argument from an evidential argument. The first claims a contradiction; the second claims that evil is strong evidence against traditional theism.
A common reply is that people cannot assume they would see every reason God might have for allowing evil.
The free will defense says moral evil comes from meaningful human choice, but it does not by itself explain all natural suffering.
Philosophers disagree about whether God’s complete knowledge of the future can fit with genuinely undetermined choices.
Open theism gives up complete detailed control, while middle knowledge tries to preserve more control by using facts about possible choices.
Other approaches say suffering may help form virtues and that evil can be overcome in a larger good, while the entry also admits that some cases remain difficult.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it brings together questions about religion, ethics, freedom, responsibility, and evidence. It teaches an important philosophical habit: distinguish a claim that something is impossible from a claim that it is improbable or difficult to believe. It also shows why one proposed answer may solve one part of a problem while creating another. Thinking carefully about providence can deepen discussion of suffering without pretending that an abstract theory removes anyone’s pain.

important_terms.definition: The belief that God guides and governs the whole world.
The challenge of explaining why evil and suffering exist if God knows everything, can do anything logically possible, and is perfectly good.
Wrongdoing that results from the choices of responsible beings.
Suffering or harm caused by nature or events not directly produced by a wrong choice.
Freedom that requires a choice not to be completely fixed by earlier conditions; it is often connected with moral responsibility.
The view that some future free choices are not yet settled truths known in advance, although God may estimate probabilities and influence circumstances.
The proposed knowledge of what a free creature would choose in any possible set of circumstances.
An explanation of why God permits evil or suffering, or how they fit into divine purposes.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between showing that an idea is possible and showing that it is likely or convincing?
Would preventing every harmful result still leave people with meaningful freedom?
Does a person’s inability to see a purpose show that no purpose exists?
Can challenges help develop virtue without making every instance of suffering acceptable?
Which seems more important in a theory of providence: God’s complete control, God’s complete knowledge, or human freedom?
